plan.question: Do religious people self-report greater well-being?
plan.estimand: Standardised regression coefficient of self-reported well-being on religiosity across 10,535 participants in 24 countries; positive means more religious people report more well-being. The option space is seeded from the analytic choices the 120 MARP teams documented.

decision_rule.metric: standardised coefficient of religiosity on well-being

steps.title: Measure religiosity
steps.description: Nine self-report items, each rescaled to 0-1; teams combined them in different ways.

options.label: Mean of all nine items
options.rationale: Uses every religiosity item the questionnaire collected.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 51 of 116 teams entered all nine items.

options.label: Mean of the seven graded items
options.rationale: Drops the two binary items (identification, denomination).
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 14 of 116 teams used these seven.

options.label: Religious self-identification only
options.rationale: A single, widely used survey item.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 13 of 116 teams used rel_3 alone.

options.label: Importance of religion to the person
options.rationale: Captures salience instead of practice or belief.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 4 of 116 teams used rel_8 and rel_9 alone.

steps.title: Measure well-being
steps.description: An 18-item scale with general, physical, psychological and social parts. Options are alternative measures of overall well-being; single facets answer a narrower question.

options.label: Overall mean of 18 items
options.rationale: The headline composite supplied with the data.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 31 of 116 teams modelled this composite.

options.label: Mean of 17 items, no sexual satisfaction
options.rationale: That item is missing for 995 participants who did not disclose.
options.spec: wb = mean of the 17 items other than wb_soc_3.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 5 of 116 teams modelled the 17 items without it.

options.label: Mean of the three subscale means
options.rationale: Weights physical, psychological and social facets equally.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 21 of 116 teams modelled the three subscale means.

options.label: Two general well-being items
options.rationale: Quality of life and satisfaction with health.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 1 team used it alone; 48 included the items in a larger set.

steps.title: Choose which participants to keep
steps.description: Some respondents failed the attention check embedded in the survey.

options.label: All participants
options.rationale: No data-driven exclusion; the full 10,535 respondents.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: the default in the data release.

options.label: Attention check passed only
options.rationale: Inattentive responding adds noise to every item.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 15 of 120 team reports mention the attention check.

steps.title: Adjust for context
steps.description: Choose which participant and country attributes enter the model.

options.label: No covariates
options.rationale: The raw association answers the question as asked.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 29 of 116 teams adjusted for nothing.

options.label: Age, gender, SES, education
options.rationale: Demographics relate to both religiosity and well-being.
options.spec: covariates = [age, gender, ses, education]; complete cases.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 56 of 116 teams adjusted for age and SES, usually with gender and education.

options.label: Demographics plus country GDP
options.rationale: Wealth differs across the 24 countries.
options.spec: covariates = [age, gender, ses, education, gdp_scaled]; complete cases.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 32 of 116 teams adjusted for GDP.

steps.title: Standardise the variables
steps.description: Convert variables to z-scores so the coefficient is a standardised beta.

options.label: Z-scores over the whole sample
options.rationale: The usual standardised beta; keeps between-country differences.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 18 of 120 team reports mention standardising.

options.label: Centred within country
options.rationale: Isolates the within-country relation; 'with and between country centering'.
options.spec: y and x centred on their country mean and scaled; m stays a global z-score.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 8 of 120 team reports mention within-country centring.

steps.title: Fit the model
steps.description: Participants are nested in 24 countries; the model family decides how that is handled.

options.label: Multilevel model, random country intercept
options.rationale: The most common choice: respondents nested in countries.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 59 of 116 teams fit a multilevel, mixed or hierarchical model; 21 reports mention random intercepts.

options.label: Pooled OLS, robust errors
options.rationale: Ignores country structure, as a simple regression does.
options.spec: OLS y ~ terms with HC3 standard errors.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 29 of 116 teams fit a plain linear regression.

options.label: OLS with country fixed effects
options.rationale: Absorbs country differences without distributional assumptions.
options.spec: OLS y ~ terms + C(country), HC3 standard errors.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: a fixed-effects specification of the same teams' linear models.

options.label: Multilevel model, random country slopes
options.rationale: Lets the religiosity slope differ by country.
options.spec: mixedlm y ~ terms, groups = country, random slope on x.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 11 of 120 team reports mention random slopes.

data.reason: Averaging the seven graded items is a common measurement of religiosity that omits the two binary items; the construct is unchanged.
A single self-identification item is widely used, though it is a coarser measure of the same construct.
Importance of religion captures salience rather than belief or practice, so it narrows the construct; defensible with a sentence of justification.
One item is missing for participants who did not disclose it, so dropping it is a reasonable handling of the item-level missingness.
Weighting the physical, psychological and social facets equally is a standard way of scoring the same well-being scale.
Two general items measure well-being directly but cover less of the scale than the full item set.
Excluding inattentive respondents is a standard data-quality rule applied before modelling.
Age, gender, socio-economic status and education relate to both religiosity and well-being; adjusting for them is standard.
Country wealth differs across the 24 countries and relates to both variables; adding GDP to the demographics is a common specification.
Centring within country isolates the within-country relation; it answers the same question on a different scale and is a recognised choice.
A pooled regression with robust errors is the simple baseline many teams used.
Country fixed effects absorb country differences without distributional assumptions and keep the same estimand.
A multilevel model with random country slopes is the standard way to let the relation vary by country.

steps.description: Nine self-report items, each rescaled to 0-1; teams combined them in different ways.

options.label: Mean of all nine items
options.rationale: Uses every religiosity item the questionnaire collected.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 51 of 116 teams entered all nine items.
options.code:
import pandas as pd


def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.copy()
    items = ["rel_1", "rel_2", "rel_3", "rel_4", "rel_5", "rel_6", "rel_7", "rel_8", "rel_9"]
    out["rel"] = out[items].mean(axis=1)
    return out

options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: the default in the data release.

steps.title: Adjust for context
steps.description: Choose which participant and country attributes enter the model.

options.label: No covariates
options.rationale: The raw association answers the question as asked.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 29 of 116 teams adjusted for nothing.
options.code:
import pandas as pd


def apply(df, ctx):
    ctx["covariates"] = []
    return df

options.label: Age, gender, SES, education
options.rationale: Demographics relate to both religiosity and well-being.
options.spec: covariates = [age, gender, ses, education]; complete cases.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 56 of 116 teams adjusted for age and SES, usually with gender and education.
options.code:
import pandas as pd


def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.dropna(subset=["age", "gender", "ses", "education"]).copy()
    ctx["covariates"] = ["age", "C(gender)", "ses", "education"]
    return out

options.label: Demographics plus country GDP
options.rationale: Wealth differs across the 24 countries.
options.spec: covariates = [age, gender, ses, education, gdp_scaled]; complete cases.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 32 of 116 teams adjusted for GDP.
options.code:
import pandas as pd


def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.dropna(subset=["age", "gender", "ses", "education", "gdp_scaled"]).copy()
    ctx["covariates"] = ["age", "C(gender)", "ses", "education", "gdp_scaled"]
    return out

steps.title: Standardise the variables
steps.description: Convert variables to z-scores so the coefficient is a standardised beta.

options.label: Z-scores over the whole sample
options.rationale: The usual standardised beta; keeps between-country differences.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 18 of 120 team reports mention standardising.
options.code:
import pandas as pd


def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.copy()
    columns = [c for c in ("wb", "rel", "norm") if c in out.columns]
    out = out.dropna(subset=columns)
    out["y"] = (out["wb"] - out["wb"].mean()) / out["wb"].std()
    out["x"] = (out["rel"] - out["rel"].mean()) / out["rel"].std()
    if "norm" in out.columns:
        out["m"] = (out["norm"] - out["norm"].mean()) / out["norm"].std()
    return out

options.label: Centred within country
options.rationale: Isolates the within-country relation; 'with and between country centering'.
options.spec: y and x centred on their country mean and scaled; m stays a global z-score.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 8 of 120 team reports mention within-country centring.
options.code:
import pandas as pd


def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.copy()
    columns = [c for c in ("wb", "rel", "norm") if c in out.columns]
    out = out.dropna(subset=columns)
    by_country = out.groupby("country", observed=True)
    for source, target in (("wb", "y"), ("rel", "x")):
        centred = out[source] - by_country[source].transform("mean")
        out[target] = centred / centred.std()
    if "norm" in out.columns:
        out["m"] = (out["norm"] - out["norm"].mean()) / out["norm"].std()
    return out

steps.title: Fit the model
steps.description: Participants are nested in 24 countries; the model family decides how that is handled.

options.label: Multilevel model, random country intercept
options.rationale: The most common choice: respondents nested in countries.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 59 of 116 teams fit a multilevel, mixed or hierarchical model; 21 reports mention random intercepts.
options.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf


def estimate(df, ctx):
    data = df.copy()
    data["country"] = data["country"].astype(str)
    covariates = list(ctx.get("covariates", []))
    terms = ["x"] + covariates
    term = "x"
    formula = "y ~ " + " + ".join(terms)
    model = smf.mixedlm(formula, data, groups=data["country"])
    fit = model.fit(reml=True, method=["powell", "lbfgs"])
    if not fit.converged:
        raise ValueError("the mixed model did not converge")
    low, high = fit.conf_int().loc[term]
    return {
        "estimate": float(fit.params[term]),
        "ci_low": float(low),
        "ci_high": float(high),
        "p_value": float(fit.pvalues[term]),
        "n": int(fit.nobs),
    }

options.label: Pooled OLS, robust errors
options.rationale: Ignores country structure, as a simple regression does.
options.spec: OLS y ~ terms with HC3 standard errors.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 29 of 116 teams fit a plain linear regression.
options.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf


def estimate(df, ctx):
    data = df.copy()
    data["country"] = data["country"].astype(str)
    covariates = list(ctx.get("covariates", []))
    terms = ["x"] + covariates
    term = "x"
    formula = "y ~ " + " + ".join(terms)
    fit = smf.ols(formula, data).fit(cov_type="HC3")
    low, high = fit.conf_int().loc[term]
    return {
        "estimate": float(fit.params[term]),
        "ci_low": float(low),
        "ci_high": float(high),
        "p_value": float(fit.pvalues[term]),
        "n": int(fit.nobs),
    }

options.label: OLS with country fixed effects
options.rationale: Absorbs country differences without distributional assumptions.
options.spec: OLS y ~ terms + C(country), HC3 standard errors.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: a fixed-effects specification of the same teams' linear models.
options.code:

import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf


def estimate(df, ctx):
    data = df.copy()

        "n": int(fit.nobs),

options.label: Multilevel model, random country slopes
options.rationale: Lets the religiosity slope differ by country.
options.spec: mixedlm y ~ terms, groups = country, random slope on x.
options.source: Hoogeveen, Sarafoglou et al. (2022), Religion, Brain & Behavior: 11 of 120 team reports mention random slopes.
options.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf


def estimate(df, ctx):
    data = df.copy()
    data["country"] = data["country"].astype(str)
    covariates = list(ctx.get("covariates", []))
    terms = ["x"] + covariates
    term = "x"
    formula = "y ~ " + " + ".join(terms)
    model = smf.mixedlm(formula, data, groups=data["country"], re_formula="~x")
    fit = model.fit(reml=True, method=["powell", "lbfgs"])
    if not fit.converged:
        raise ValueError("the mixed model did not converge")
    low, high = fit.conf_int().loc[term]
    return {
        "estimate": float(fit.params[term]),
        "ci_low": float(low),
        "ci_high": float(high),
        "p_value": float(fit.pvalues[term]),
        "n": int(fit.nobs),
    }

report.question: Do religious people self-report greater well-being?
report.robustness_design_note: uniform random sample of the grid: 12 draws (each decision picks each of its options equally), 10 distinct results; independent of the beam search

estimand_changes.label: Age, gender, SES, education
estimand_changes.detail: changes the covariates of the model (adds age, education, gender, ses): adjusted versus unadjusted answers a different question, so this is an estimand change, not a re-analysis of the same quantity

estimand_changes.label: Demographics plus country GDP
estimand_changes.detail: changes the covariates of the model (adds age, education, gdp_scaled, gender, ses): adjusted versus unadjusted answers a different question, so this is an estimand change, not a re-analysis of the same quantity

estimand_changes.label: OLS with country fixed effects
estimand_changes.detail: changes the covariates of the model (adds country): adjusted versus unadjusted answers a different question, so this is an estimand change, not a re-analysis of the same quantity

report.narrative: With the default choices, religiosity goes with higher well-being: beta = 0.140 (95% CI 0.119 to 0.160), p < 0.001, n = 10,535, so the verdict is POSITIVE ASSOCIATION. Borges ran 38 universes: the baseline, 13 single changes and 24 combinations. No flip was found: all 38 universes keep the verdict (design-weighted robustness 100%); the estimate runs from 0.060 to 0.150, the lowest interval bound is 0.043 and the largest p-value is p < 0.001. The 110 research teams that reported a standardised effect range from 0.007 to 0.354 (median 0.120), and 110 of them (100%) have an interval above zero.
caveats: 2 universes could not run and are left out of the robustness figure.

Robustness headline is design-weighted (100%): uniform random sample of the grid: 12 draws (each decision picks each of its options equally), 10 distinct results; independent of the beam search. The share among the explored universes is 100%, but the beam search samples the universes that are closest to flipping, so that figure leans toward flips.

The robustness figure comes from a uniform random sample of the option grid, which is built from the choices the teams documented; the share among all explored universes leans toward flips because the search chases them. Neither is a population estimate.
Standardised coefficients describe an association in a convenience sample of 24 countries; they do not show that religion causes well-being.
2 universes failed to run and are excluded.
